naphtha.c: NAPHTHA ?, are Wheals, Ulcers or Pimples a - bout the Internal Parts of the Mouth; as also a - bout the Ventricle and Guts, which when they come to be ripe, fall off by piece - meal, and are often accompanied with a Fever in those of riper Years. Infants are often fubjed to the Aphtha, they begin in the Gums, and by degrees spread over the whole Palate and Mouth; if they seize the Epiglottis and the upper parts of the Throat, the Child seldom recovers. These are called Aph - tha of Celfus.

ntereoramineum.c: NTEREOR AMINEUM, or Interfemineum, the fame with Perineum.

nadir.c: NADIR, is that Point of the Heavens seeming - ly under the Earth, which is Diametrically oppo - site to the Point diredrly over our Head, the Zenith; so that they are both as it were the Poles of the Horizon, and distant from it oh each side Degrees, and consequently fall upon the Me - ridian, one above, the other under the Earth; and whatever Distance one of them has from the Equator, and one of the Poles of the World; the fame on the contrary, has the other from the opposite Pole, and adverse part of the Equator.

naiantornatant.c: NAIANT, or Natant, ( i. e. Swimming ) is the proper Term in Heraldry, to Blazon Fishes in an Escutcheon, when they are drawn in an Horizontal Posture, Sess - wife, or Tranfverfly across the Escutcheon but if they are Erect, ’ tis called Hauriant.

nailingofcannon.c: NAILING of Cannon, is the driving of a NaU, of Iron Spike, by force into the Touch - hole of a Piece of Artillery, so as to render it useless to the Enemy.

naissant.c: NAISSANT, i. e. Nascent, just new Born; the Herald ’ s Term for a Lyon, or other Beast, ap - bearing to be issuing or coming out of the middle f any Sense, or other Ordinary for if it come out from the lower Line of the Ordinary, they call it IJfuant.

nakedfire.c: NAKED Fire, a Term used by the Chymifts, for an open Fire, or one not pent or closed up. NAPIERS Bones. See Nepers.

narcosis.c: NARCOSIS, is a privation of Sense, as in a Palfie, &c. or in taking of Opium, cc. whence strong Opiate Medicines are frequently called. NARCOTICKS, or Narcotick Medicines. NAS ALIA, the fame that Errhina. NASCALIA, are little Globular Bodies which On some Occasions, are put into the Neck of the Matrix; they are made of the fame Substance as the Feffaria. See Peffaria.

nasi.c: NASI Or, is a thin but solid Bone, which makes the upper part of the Nose; it ’ s upper end is join ’ d to the Os Frontis by the Sutura Transverse - lis: One of its Sides joins its feiiow, and its lower is joined to the Os Maxillare, upon its lower end the Cartilages of the Nostrils are fast - ned; externally it is smooth, but internally it is rough.

natescerebri.c: NATES Cerebri, are two round Prominences in the Brain, behind the Beds of the Optick Nerves, which grow to the upper part of the Marrowy Substance they are small in Men, and larger in Brutes.

natka.c: NATKA, is a great soft Tumor, with Pain and N A A Colour, which grows most usually in the Back, but sometimes in the Shoulders; its Root is seen - der, yet it encreases so prodigiously, that it will grow as big as a Melon, or a Gourd; it is made of fat matter, and therefore ought to be reckon - ed amongst the Steatomata. See Steatomata, Blanchard.

nature.c: NATURE: This Word has usually these Signi - fications. First, and more strictly, it is taken for a pe - cular Disposition of Farts in some particular Body as we fay, it is the Nature of Fishes to live in the Water. Secondly, It is taken more largely for the U - universal Disposition of all Bodies And in this sense ’ tis nothing else, but the Divine Providence, forasmuch as it governs and directs all things by certain Buies and Laws, accommodated to the Na - tures of things. Thirdly, It is taken for the EJfence of any thing, not Corporeal, with the Attributes belonging to it: Thus we fay. That it is the Nature of God to be Good, and the Nature of the Soul to Think.

NATURE. Besides the three Senses of this Word mentioned in Vol. I. it is fomedmes used for this vast Machine of the XJnive fe, the wife ' Produdion of Almighty God, consisting of a great number of lesser Machines, every one of which is adjusted by the fame Wisdom in Number, Weight and Measure. Laws of Nature, signifie those Laws of Motion by which Natural Bodies are governed in all their Adions upon one another, and which they invio - lably observe in all the Changes that happen in the i N A y the Natural State of Things. An Account of these Laws see in Motion. Sir Isaac Newton at the End of his excellent Op - ticks ( At. Edit. ) observes, That Universal N a - ture is very Simple and Uniform in its Operations. All the Motions of the Heavenly Bodies are caused by that Attracting Force, Impulse or Power which we call Gravitation; and which is mutual amongst all those Bodies. AH the lesser Motions of the Par - titles or Corpuscles of Matter whereby Bodies ad on one another, are eflfeded also, by some Attract - ing and Repelling Force; which is mutual and re - ciprocal amongst them. The Vis Inertice, is a Principle purely pajjive, by which Bodies persist in their Hate of Reft or Mo - tion, whereby they receive Motion from others e - qual or proportionable to the moving Force; and whereby they rejifi as much as they are rejijied. But from this Principle alone there never could have been any such thing as Motion, any where in theUniverfe. There is a necessity of supposing some other Principle to be the Origen ot Motion, and its Constitution too: for from the various Compositions of two Motions, ’ tis plain that there cannot be always the fame quantity of Motion in the World. For if two Globes, conceded toge - ther by a slender Thread, be supposed to revolve with an uniform Motion round their common Centre of Gravity; and at the fame time that Centre should move on Uniformity also in a Right Line coincident with the Plane of the Globes Or - bits: Then will the Summ of the Motions of those two Globes, whenever they happen to be both in the Right Line described by the common Centre of Gravity, be - greater than the Summ of their Motions czji be, when they are in a Line at Right Angles to that. By which Instance ’ tis apparent, that Motion is producible and destructible. But from the Tenacity and Attrition of the Particles of Fluid Bodies, and the Imbecillity of the Elastick force in solid Bodies, we may conclude, that the course of Nature tends more to the Destruction than the Production of Motion; and indeed it is conti - nually decreasing, for Bodies that are either so perfedly hard, or throughly soft, as to have no E - elasticity, cannot be reverberated back from one a - nother, and from their Impenetrability only it would follow that their Motion would stop, and terminate. If therefore there were any such things as the Imaginary Vortexes of Des Cartes, their Mo - tion must be continually decreasing, and at last rust quite cease. Since therefore Motion is thus continually decreasing in the Univerle, we must have recourse to some Active Principles, to encrease and preserve it; vi. to such as the Cause of Gra - city and Fermentation: by the former of which the Planets and Comets perpetually move in their Orbits, and Bodies by descending gain a great Velocity or large quantity of Motion; and by the latter, the Heart and Blood of Animals is pre - served in Motion and Warmth: The Internal parts of the Earth are perpetually getting Heat,. many Bodies burn and shine, Volcanoes and Earth - quakes are produced, and the Sun it self preserves his Light and Heat, and warms and cherilhes all things ': For we find very little Motion in the World ( except what is voluntary in free A gents J but what depends on these Adive Causes. So that after well considering and understand - ing these things, our admirable Author whose Piety and Goodness is as eminent as his profound Mathematick Learning and Penetration into Uni -, versal Nature ) concludes, that our Perfectly Good, molt Wife and Almighty Creator, did in the be - ginning of the World, create Matter so as that its Original Particles, from whence all Corporeal Na - tures were to arise, were solid, firm, impenetrable, perfectly passive and moveable; and that they were made of such Magnitudes and Figures, and endued with such Properties, and in that Number and Quantity as was proportionable to the Space in which they were afterwards to move, in order to the most effedual obtaining of those Ends and Purposes for which they were created. And these Original Primary Particles being per - fectly solid, must be much more hard and firm than any Bodies that can be made out of them with Pores, hidden Meatufes or Vacuities inter - Iperfed; that is, so perfectly hard and firm, that they can never be worn away or diminished: for ’ tis not reasonable to suppose that there should be any Force or Power in the ordinary course of Na - ture, that can divide that into more parts, which God in the first Creation of things, hath made one. As long therefore as these Original Particles re - main entire, there may for ever be Bodies made or composed of them; which still have the fame Nature and Texture: But if these can be broken, worn away or diminished, then the Nature of Cor - portal things which is dependent on these might be changed. Earth and Water composed of ei - ther such Particles as have been worn or broken, ' or of their Fragments, could not have at this day, the. fame Nature and Texture, that original Earth and Water which was composed of these Particles I when they were found and entire. Wherefore ! that the Nature of Things should last, and their i Natural Course continue the fame; all the chang - J es made in Bodies must arise only from the vari - ous Separations, new Conjunctions and Motions of i these Original Particles. For mix ’ d or compound - i ed Bodies are broken or destroyed, not by the ! breaking to pieces of their Solid Original Particles, but by separating them one from another, and I disposing them in those places where they touch ’ d one another but in a little part of their Surface. And these Original Particles, seem not only to have in them the Vis Inertia and all those Pa / five Laws of Motion which necessarily arise from thence; but receive also Motion continually from certain Active Principles; vi. such as Gravity the cause of Fermentation and of the Coheficn of the Parts of Matter. And these Principles are not to be considered as Occult Qualities which are feigned to arise from the Specifick Forms of things, but as the ) Universal Laws of Nature by which things them - selves are formed. For that there are really such Principles, the various Phenomena of Nature do demonstrate, tho ’ what their Causes are hath not yet been explained: For to assert that the fever al Species of Things are endued with Specifick ! Occult Qualities by which they have a certain force or power in adding, is in reality to fay nothing. But from the Phenomena of Nature to derive two or three general Principles of Motion; and from thence to explain how the Properties and A dions of all Corporeal Things may be deduced from those Principles, would be a very great Progress in Na - tural Philosophy, although the Causes of those Principles should be yet undiscovered.

naturalization.c: NATURALIZATION, is when an Alien born Subject, is made the King ’ s Natural j and this mull be done by Adfc of Parliament. Vide Denizens.

naturalhorizon.c: NATURAL Horizon, the fame with., Sensible Horizon. See Horizon.

naturalphilosophy.c: NATURAL Philosophy, is the fame with what is usually call ’ d Physicks, vi. That Science which contemplates the Powers of Nature, the Proper - ties of Natural Bodies, and their mutual AdHon one upon another.

naviculareos.c: NAVICULARE Os, called also Cymbiforme, is the third Bone in each Foot, in that Part of it which immediately succeeds the Leg.

navigation.c: NAVIGATION, is the Art of Sailing, where - by the Mariner is inftrudled how to guide a Ship from one Port to another, the shortest and fafeft way, and in the shortest Time: And this is two - fold; either Improper, Which is called Coasting, in which the Places are at no great distance one from a - nother, and the Ship fails usually in fight of Land, and is within Soundings. Now for the Performance of this, there is required a good Knowledge of the Lands, the Use of the Com - pass, the Lead, or Sounding - Line, and such Books as Butters, See. Navigation Proper, is where the Voyage is per - form ’ d in the vast Ocean, out of fight of all Land; and here is necessary not only the Knowledge of ' the Lead, Compass, &c. but fthe Master must be a thro ’ Sailor or Artist, and understand well Mer eater's Charts, Azimuth and Amplitude Compass r Leg - Line, N E G N E P Log - Line, and all good Instruments for Celejlial Vbjervations that can be used at Sect. And how to perform the several Parts and Cafes of this Art, you will find under the Word Plain, and Merca - tors Sailing.

nauseousnessornausea.c: NAUSEOUSNESS, or Nausea, Loathing, is an earnest Endeavour to Vomit, with Sickness and Uneasiness.

nauticalplanisphere.c: NAUTICAL Planisphere, is a Description of the Terrestrial Globe upon a Plane, for the Use of Mariners; and is either, i. The Plane Chart, as they call it, Where the Parallels of Latitude are all of the fame length with the Meridians j and which therefore is very erroneous, except in Ihort Voyages, and near the Equator: Or, z. Wright's, commonly called Mercator s Chart, where the Meridians are increased in Proportion,, as the Parallels Ihorten: That is, as the Secants of the Arks contained between the Point of La - titude, and the Equator. NE Admittas, is a Writ directed to the Bi - slip, at the Suit of one who is Patron of any Church and he doubts that the Bishop will Col - late one his Clerk, or admit another Clerk pre - sented by another Man to the fame Benefice: Then he that doubts it, shall have this Writ, to forbid the Bishop to Collate or Admit any to that Church.

nebuloseaterm.c: NEBULOSE, a Term, in Heraldry, when the out - Line of any Bordure, Ordinary, &c. is of this Form, f. e. resembling something of the Figure of Clouds. QSWSWl

nebulousstars.c: NEBULOUS Stars, are certain fixed Stars of a dull, pale, and obfeurifh Light.

necrosis.c: NECROSIS, is a Black and Blue Mark in any part of the Body.

negativepregnant.c: NEGATIVE Pregnant, is when an Adion, In - formation, or such like, is brought against one, and the Defendant Pleads in Bar of the Adion, or otherwise a Negative Plea, which is not so special an Answer to the Action, but that it in - cludes also an Affirmative: As if a Man being impleaded to have done a thing on such a Day, or in such a Place, denieth that he did it Modo & forma declamata; which implieth nevertheless. That in some fort he did it: Or if a Man be said to have alienated Land in Fee, and he faith, he hath not alienated in Fee, this is Negative Pregnant; for tho ’ it be true that he hath not lie - nated in Fee, yet it may be, he hath made an Estate in Taile.

negativequantitiesinalgebra.c: NEGATIVE Quantities in Algebra, are such as have before them the

negativesign.c: NEGATIVE Sign, and which are suppo - fed to be less than nothing. These are dired - ly contrary to Positive, Affirmative, or Real Quantities. NE injufle vexes, is a Writ which lies for a Te - nant that is Distrained by his Lord for other Ser - vices than he ought to make, and is a Prohibiti - on to the Lord in it self, commanding him not to Distrain.

neipetides.c: NEIPE TIDES, written alio Nepe or Neep, are those Tides ( when the Moon is in the middle of the second and lalt Quarter ) which are opposite to the Spring - Tides and as the highest of the Spring - Tides is three Days after the Full or Change, so the lowest of the Neep is four Days before the Full or Change; and then the Seamen fay, that it is Deep Neep: Also when a Ship wants Wa - ter, so that ffie cannot get out of a Harbour, off from the Ground, or out of the Dock, the Seamen fay file is Neiped.

neomenium.c: NEOMENIUM, signifies only the New Moon, or Change.

NEPHELiE, are small White Spots upon the Eyes; also little Clouds, as it were, that swim in the middle of the Urine; likewise little white Spots in the Surface of the Nails like little Clouds.

nephriticks.c: NEPHRITICKS, are Medicines against the Diseases of the Reins.

nephritis.c: NEPHRITIS, is a Pain in the Reins, proceed - ing either from an ill Disposition, or an Inflam - motion, or from the Stone and Gravel, accoy - panied with Vomiting and Stretching of the Thigh. Blanchard.

nephros.c: NEPHROS, is a Kidney, one on each side of the Abdomen, placed about the Loins under the Liver and Spleen; it is ftiaped like a Kidney - Bean: Its Substance is made up of a great Com - any of little Pipes. On both sides it receives the Serum from the Glandules which border upon the Arteries, and carries it to the little Bodies in the Reins called Caruncula Papillares, ( which fee ) that so it may be discharged by the Pelvis i the V - ureters, the Bladder, &c. See Irenes.

nerve.c: NERVE, is an Organical Similar Part of an Human Body, being also of a fibrous round, long, white porous Substance, and whose Use is to con - very the Animal Spirits lb, as to make the Parts of the Body moveable andfenfible. The Nerves are supposed to contain a Three - fold Substance; the Innermost of which is white and medullary, and is thought to proceed from the Medulla Cerebri; the other two are supposed to arise from the Meninges of the Brain: Of which the middle and lester comes from the Pia mater, and the outer and harder from the Dura mater, All the Nerves take their Rife from the Me - dull oblongata cerebri, either within the Skull, or from its Continuation, when it becomes the Med dull spinalis. Diemerbroeck reckons Pairs or Conjugations of Nerves, besides the Nervus fins pari - and he reckons that Nine Pair of these a - rife ' within the Skull, and the other he faith come from the Medulla spinalis, through the Per - forations of the Vertebra; which he subdivided into the Eight Cervical Pairs, the Twelve Thorax - deal, the Five that come from the Region of the Loins, and the other Five which come from the Os sacrum; to which the Nervus fine pari is to be added, which arises from the End of the Spinal Marrow, and which feme have taken for a kind of Ligament. - The Nerves do ordinarily accompany the Arte - ries thro ’ all the Body, that by the Pulse of the Arteries, the Animal Spirits may be kept warm and moving. The Nerves have also Blood - Vessels attending them, which are spread usually on their Coats; and do also sometimes run in among the Medul - lay Fibres, as may be seen ih those of the Re - tin. Where - ever a Nerve fends out a Branch, or re - chives one from another, there is commonly a Ganglio or Plexus, as you may fee at the Origin of all the Nerves in the Medulla spinalis, and in many Places of the Body.

nervusinbotanicks.c: NERVUS, in Botanicks, signifies a long Fi - lament or rigid String, which runs across or length ways in the Leaf of a Plant. And thus, because there are Five such Nerves or Filaments running long ways in the Leaves of one kind of Plantane, that Plant hath been called Quinque nerve.

nettings.c: NETTINGS, in a Ship, are a set of Grate made with small Ropes, and seized together with Rope - yarn; and are laid in the Waft of a Ship sometimes, to serve instead of Gratings.

neurodes.c: NEURODES, is a fort of lingering Fever, so called by the Learned Dr. Willis; because that the Nervous Juice, departing from its own right natural Gratis, becomes the Occasion of an Atrophy.

neurology.c: NEUROLOGY, is an accurate Description of, orDifcourfe on, the Nerves of an Human Body.

neuroticks.c: NEUROTICKS, are Remedies against the Dis - eafes of the Nerves.

neurotomy.c: NEUROTOMY, is an Anatomical Section of the Nerves, for the Benefit f the Patient; and sometimes also a pricking of the Nerves by unskil - ful Bleeding, &c.

neutral.c: NEUTRAL. Mf. Boyle calls feme kind of Spirits which he could distil from Tartar, and feme ponderous Woods, by this Name of Neu - tral Spirits, as also Adiaphorous and Anonymous; because he found them very different in Quality and Nature from either the Acid, Vinous, or V - rinous Spirits. For the way of making it, " fee Adiaphorous.

nicheinarchitecture.c: NICHE, in Architecture, is a Cavity left de feignedly in the Wall of a Building, to place a Statue in.

nictitansmemhrana.c: NICTITANS Memhrana, is a thin Purplifli or Reddish Membrane or Film, which several Beasts and Birds have to cover or Afield their Eyes from Dust, &c. they can draw it over their Eyes at pleasure, and ’ tis so very much thinner I. thus N I T han the Eye - lid, that they can fee pretty Well thro ’ it.

nihilornichil.c: NIHIL, or Nichil, is a Word which the She - riff answers, that is opposed concerning Debts il - leviable, and that are nothing worth, by rea - fon of the insufficiency of the Parties from whom they are due.

nihil.c: NIHIL dich, is a failing to put in Answer to the Plea of the Plaintiff by the Day aligned, which if a Man omit, Judgment passeth against him of Course by Nihil dicit; that is, because he says nothing in his own Defence, why it ihould not. Nihil capias per Breve, is the Judgment given against the Plaintiff, either in Bar of his Adion, or in Abatement of his Writ. Nihil capias per billam, the fame with Nihil capias per Breve.

nippers.c: NIPPERS are small Ropes in a Ship about a Fathom or two long, with a little Truck at one end, and sometimes only a Wale knot j their Use is to help hold off the Cable from the Main or Jeer Capstan, when the Cable is so slimy, so wet, or so great, that they cannot strain it to hold it off with their bare Hands.

nisiprius.c: NISI Prius, is a Writ Judicial, which Lieth in Case, where the Jury is Impannell ’ d, and return ’ d before the Justices, the one Party or the other requesting to have this Writ for the case of the Country, whereby the Sheriff is willed to cause the Inquest to come before the Justices in the fame County at their coming; and it is called a Writ of the Nisi prius, of these two Words, where - by the Sheriff is commanded to bring to Wefimin - Jler the Men ImpanneH ’ d at a certain Day, or be - fore the Justices of the next Assizes, Nisi die Luna apud talem locum prius venerint, &c.

nitre.c: NITRE, the fame with Salt Petre. Some are mighty fond of the Notion of a Volatile Nitre, which abounds in the Air; and they attribute a - abundance of Phanomena to the Operation of the Nitrous Particles in the Air. That the Air abounds with Saline Particles, is in oft certain for being filled continually with Effluvia from the Earth and Sea, it must needs have from both a great Quantity of Saline Cor - muscles; and these will be of different Kinds ac - cording to the variety of those Salts from whence they are derived. But why these Ihould be most - ly supposed of a Nitrous Nature, is not so easie to prove; for Salt Petre is by no means found in a greater Quantity than the other Salts ( else - cially common Salt; ) nor is it of a much more Volatile Nature than they, nor capable of being raised more eafi'ly, or by a lesser heat. But since Soot, and that which produces it, Smoak, is found to abound very much with a truly Vola - tile Salt; and since such a kind of Salt is - pro - duced frequently by the Putrefaction of Animal and Vegetable Bodies, there is good reason to luppole the Air may abound with Salts of this kind: As; also with many decompounded ones or very different Kinds and Natures, and to which no proper Name can well be assigned and there - fore they have been called Anonymous, by Mr. Boyle and many others.

noctambulo.c: NOCTAMBULO, or NoBambuius, is one who walks m his Sleep;

nocturnal.c: NOCTURNAL, is anlnftrument made of Box, Ivory, or Brass, divided en both sides, to take the Altitude or Depression of the Pole - Star, in rested to the Pole it self, in order to find the Latitude and nearly the Hour of the Night.

NOCTURNAL. There are several forts of NoBumals, of which feme may be Projections of the Sphere; such as the Hemispheres or Plani - spheres on the Plane of the Equinoctial; but the Seamen use only two, and the manner of using either is the fame. One of them is fitted for the Pole - Star and the first of the Guards of the Little Bear; and the other for the Pole - Star and the Guards or Pointers ( as some call them ) of the Great Bear, The Instrument consists of three Parts or Pieces; ! the largest of which hath a Handle to hold it by ! when you would observe; and opposite to the Handle there is a small Tcoth or Point, which ( if it be made for the Little Bear ) Hands against the, th of April; but if f r the Great Bear against the th of February which are the times of the Year when those Stars come to the Meridian at at Night On this bigger Part or Piece then are two Circles described; the Outermost hath the Months and their Days, and the Innermost hath the Hours of a Natural Day; on the backside of this Piece also are the Points of the Compass designed, and marked with their initial Letters. he second part of the Nodurnal hath two Circles described on it; of which the outermost is divided into. equal parts, for the Days of the Moon ’ s Age; and the innermost into Hours: and at the beginning of the Days of the Moon ’ s Age, and at XII, there is a Tooth to be fet to the Day of the Month in the upper part. The third part is an Index with a Fiducial Edge Bluing from the Centre; and must be so long, that a good part of it may extend beyond the outermost or biggest piece. These three Parts are so ordered that by means of a small hollow Brass Socket they are made to move about the Centre of the Instruments. See the Fig. annexed. . To find the Hour of the Night, To do which, fet the Tooth to the middle pare of the Day of the Month, and then turning the foreside of the Instrument towards you, hold it up towards the North and incline the upper part to - ward you, till thro ’ the Hole in the middle you can see the Pole - Star; there hold it fast, and turn the long Index about till by its Edge you can fee either the first of the Guards of the Little Bear or the Pointers of the Great Bear ( according as the Instrument is made ) and then shall the Edge of F the the Index or Ruler, in the innermost Circle of the I middle part shew you the true Hour of the Night. . To find on what - Point of the Compass the Guards are. This will appear on the backside of the Noctur - nal, after you have found the Hour of the Night, as above; for the Index will be on the fame Point of the Compass as the Guards really are. . To find at what Hour the Moon will he full South on any Day of her Age. Seek the Moon ’ s Age in the outermost Circle of the middle Piece, and then right against it in the innermost Piece, is the Hour required. Thus if the Moon be Days old, you will find file will be on the Meridian at Hours, Min.

nocturnalarl.c: NOCTURNAL Arl, is tha. t Space in the Heavens which the Sun, Moon, or Stars, run thro from their Rising to their Setting.

nocturlabe.c: NOCTURLABE, is an Instrument uled to find how much the North Star is higher or lower than the Pole at all Hours of the Night.

noctiluca.c: NOCTILUCA, is one of the two kinds of Phos - phorus; the former of which, such as the Bolo - ' nian Stone, Hermetic f Phosphorus Balduini, See. will not Ihine, except first exposed to the Sun - beams, but this kind of NoBiluca, is a self - she ning Substance, which requires the being exp - fed to no Light to render it Luminous: As the Phosphorus made of Urine, &c. which see in Phgfi phorus. Mr. Boyle in his Book of the Aerial NoBiluca " reckons three of these NoBiluca. . The Gummous, Confident or Constant one, ( as some Germans call it which is in the Form of a Confident Body. . The Liquid NoBiluca, which probably is only the former dissolved in a proper Liquor. The Aerial NoBiluca, because it would im - mediately begin to Ihine, on being exposed to the open Air. See the Process for this last, P, of the aforementioned Book, which being tsniefa the fame with that of the Phosphorus, commonly made out of Humane Urine, I have omitted. See Phosphorus.

nodesinastronomy.c: NODES, in Astronomy, signifie the Points of In - teifedfcion of tho Orbit of the Sun, or any Pla net, with the Ecliptick, so that the Point where a Planet passes over the Ecliptick,, out of Sou - thern into Northern Latitude, is called the North Node: And where it descends from North to South, f is the South - Node - which Nodes ( accord - ding to some ) change their Places in the Zodi - ack, like the Planets: But Sir If. Newton proves Proj.. Lib.. that the Nodes of all the Pla - nets Orbits ( as well as their Aphelia ) are at Reft.

nodulus.c: NODULUS, No. dus, is a Bag of such suitable Ingredients as the Disease requires, pur into Beer or Wine, the Tincture whereof the Patient is to drink.

nodusornode.c: NODUS or Node, in Dialing, in a certain Point in the Axis or Cock of the Dial, by the Ibadow of which, either the Hour of the Day in Dials without Furniture, or the Parallels of the Suns Declination, his Place in the Ecliptick., the Italian or Babylonijh Hours, See. are Ihown, in such Dials as have Furniture. Tis an easie thing, and sometimes of good use, to make Dials which Shall Ihew the Hour of the Day by an Hole or NODUS, O N

nodus.c: NODUS. One Method of which, Mr. Collins j at the end of his Sector on a Quadrant, gives as follows. Fir It, Draw an Horizontal Dial for the, Lati - tude proposed: Then by the help of the Sun ’ s Azimuth ( which may be found by a Quadrant, or by knowing the Hour of the Day by that Horizontal Dial, draw a true Meridian from the Hole or Modus proposed, both above in the Ceil - ing, and below on the Walls and Floor of the Room; so that if a Right Line were extended from the said Hols or Nodus to any Point in any of those Lines, it would be in the Meridian Cir - cle of the World. Next, fix the end of a Thread in the Centre of the Hole or Nodus, and move the other end thereof up or down in the said Meridian drawn on the Ceiling or Wall, until by applying the side of a Quadrant to that Thread, it is found to be elevated equal to the Latitude of the Place, then that Thread is directly situated parallel to the Axis of the World, and the Point where the end of that Thread touch th the Meridian either on the Ceiling or Wall, is that Point in the. direct Axis fought for; wherein fix one end of the Thread, which Thread will be of present Use in projecting the Hour - Points in any. place pro - poled. Then place the Centre of the Horizontal Dial, in the Centre of the Hole or Nodus, and situate it exactly parallel to the Horizon, and its Meridian in the Meridian of the World, ( which may easily be done, if at the Instant you know the true Hour of the Day ) then take the Thread whose end is fixed in a Point in the direct Axe, and move it to and fro, until the Thread doth inter - pose between your Eye, and the Hour - Line on the Horizontal Dial, and keeping your Eye in that Position, make a Point, or Mark where you please, so that the Thread may interpose between that Point and your Eye; which Point lo found, will ihew the true time of the Day at that Hour all the Year long, the Sun Ihining thereon, so will the Point and the said Thread serve to Ihew the Hour, instead of an Hour - Line. In like manner, the Thread fixed in the Axis may be again moved to and fro, until the. Thread doth interpose between the Eye and any other Hour - Line desired on the Horizontal Dial, and then ( as before ) make another Point or Mark in any place at pleasure, by projecting a Point from the Eye, so that the Thread interpose between that Point to be made, and the Eye, so will that Point so found Ihew the true time of the Day for the fame Hour that the Hour - Line did on the Horizontal Dial, which was shadow ’ d by the Thread. Tfius you may proceed, ( by the help of that Thread and the several Hour - Lines on the Hori - ontal Dial, ) to find the other Hour - Points, which must have the fame Numbers fet to them as the Hour - Lines on the Horizontal Dial have. Otherwise to make a Dial from a Hole in any Pane of Glass in the Window, and to graduate the Hour - Lines on the Ceiling, Floor, j c. that Hole is supposed to be the Centre of the Hori - ontal Dial, and being true placed, the Stile thereof, if supposed continued, will run into the Point in the Meridian. of the Ceiling before found, here a head is to be fixed; then let one ex - tend a Thread i aliened in the Centre of the Ho rizontal Dial, parallel to the Horizon over each respective. Hour - Line, and holding it Heady, let another extend the Thread fastned in the Meri - dian in the Ceiling, along by the Edges of the Horizontal Thread, which will find divers Points on the Ground, thro ’ which, ifHour - Lines. be drawn, ' the Sun. Ihining thro ’ the Hole in the Pane of Glass, will ihew the Time of the Day. For the Points that will be thus found on the Beam or Tranlome, the Thread fixed in the Ceiling, or instead of it a piece of Tape there fixed must be moved so up and down, that the Spot of the Sun may shine upon it; and being extended to the Tranfome or Beam, graduated with the Hour - Lines, it there Ihews the Time of the Day. Note, That twill be convenient to have that Pane of Glass dark ’ d, thro ’ which that Spot is to Ihine. In like manner may a Dial be made from d Nail - head, a Knot in a String tied any where a - cross, or from any Pin driven to the Bar of the Window, and the Hour - Lines graduated upon the Tranfome or Board underneath. To make a Reflected Dial on the Ceiling of the Room, is only the contrary of this, by sup poling the Horizontal Dial, with its Stile, to be turned downwards, and run into the true Me - ridian on the Ground, where the Thread is to - be fixed, and to be extended along the former Horizontal Thread ( held over the respective Hours ) upward, to find divers Points in the Ceiling.

noli.c: NOLI me t angers, is a fort of Canker in the Face, especially above the Chin; them arises a Tu - mour or Ulcer about the Mouth and Nose, like an exulcerated Canker, which grows slowly at the beginning, like a little Pimple; it remains a whole Year, otherwise is left troublesome than a Canker, which gnaws and eats more in one Day, than a Noli me t anger e, doth in a'Month.

nombril.c: NOMBRIL ( or Navel, Point in an Elcutcheom See the Word Escutcheon.

nome.c: NOME, are deep and putrid Ulcers in the Mouth. Blanchard.

nomeinalgebra.c: NOME, in Algebra, is any Quantity with d Sign prefixed to it, and by which ’ tis usually con - necked With some other Quantity, and then the whole is called a Binomial, or Trinomial, &c, Thus a - f - b is called a Binomial, whose Names are a and b and a - j - b c is a Trimoniai, whose Names are a, b, and c, cc.

nonabilityinlaw.c: NONABILITY, in Law is an Exception ta - ken against the Plaintiff or Defendant, upon some cause why he cannot commence Suit in Law, as Pramunire, Outlawry, Prcfejl in Religion, Excom - municate, or a Stranger born, which last holds only in Actions real and mix ’ d, and not in Per - synal, except he be a Stranger and an Enemy. The Civilians fay. That such a Man hath not Per - fonamflandi injudicio,

non.c: NON compos mentis That is, not of found Memory or Understanding of such in Common Law they reckon: First, An Ideot Born. Secondly, He that by Accident wholly lofeth his Memory and Understanding. Thirdly, A Lunatick, that hath Lucida inter - villa sometimes has Understanding, and some - times not. . He that by his own Ad for a time depri - ved ! himself of his right Senses, as a Drunkard j but this last kind ( hall give no Privilege to him or his Heirs.
NON diftringendo, is a Writ comprising un - der it divers Particulars, according to divers Cafes. See Tab. of Orig. Reg. Verb, non distrain - gendo.

NON el Culpabilis, in Law, signifies the gent - ral Plea to an Adion of Trespass, whereby the Defendant doth absolutely deny the Sad imputed to him by the Plaintiff whereas in other Special Cafes the Defendant but allegeth some reason in his own Defence.
NON eft fallum, is an Answer to a Declara - tion, whereby a Man denieth that to be his Deed, whereupon he is Impleaded.

NON - Natural Things, or the Non - Natural Causes of Diseases, as the Physicians reckon them are fix, vi. The Air, Meat and Drink, Sleep and want of Sleep, the Motions and Repose of the Body, the Retention, or Evacuation of the Excre - ments and Recrements of it, and the Passions of the Mind.
NON - Organical Part of an Animal, is that whereto fomeUfc is only appropriated, but ho A dion, asaGriftle, Bone, Foot, &c.

NON omit. propt. aliquam libertat. is a Writ that lies where the Sheriff returns upon a Writ to him directed, that he hath sent to the Bayliff of such a Franchise which hath the return of Writs, and he hath not served the Writ, then the Plain - tiff shall have this Writ directed to the Sheriff to enter into the Franchise, and execute the King ’ s Process himself. Also the Sheriff shall warn the Bayliff, That [ he be before the Justices at the Day mentioned in the Writ, and if he come not, then all the Judicial Writs, during the fame Plea, issue - ing, shall be Writs of Non Omittas, and the She - riff shall execute the fame.

NON - Reftdence, in Law, is applied to such Spi - ritual Persons as are not Resident n, but do ab ? sent themselves for the space of a Month or two, at several times in one Year from their Benefices, for Personal Reftdence is required of Ecclesiastical Persons upon their Cures.

NON - Suit, in Law, is Renouncing of the Suit by the Plaintiff or Demandant, most commonly upon the Discovery of some Error or Defed, when the Matter is so far proceeded in, as that the Jury is ready at the Bar to deliver their Verdid. The Civilians term it, Litis renunciationem. And in what Cafes a Man cannot be Non - Suit, see the Statute of H.. cap..

nonageaterminlaw.c: NONAGE, a Term in Law, signifying all that time of a Man ’ s Age, under One and twenty Years in some Cafes, and Fourteen in others, as Marriage.

nonagesimaldegree.c: NONAGESIMAL Degree, is the highest Point, - or th Degree of the Meridian. MoNCTMMf / /

nonclaim.c: NONCLAIM, a ' Term in Law, signifying the Omission or Negled, of him that ought to chal - ledge his Right within a time limited, by which Negled he is either barr ’ d of his Right, as at this Day upon Nonclam within five Years after a Fine, and Right to him accrued or of his En - try by his Descent, for want of Claim, within five Years after the Dijf elfin.

nones.c: NONES, of a Month, are the next Days after the Kalends, which is the first Day. In March, May, June and October, the Romans accounted fix Days of the Nones, but in all the reft of the Months but four. They had this Name probably because they were always Days inclusively, from the first of the Nones to the Ides i. e. reckoning inclusively both those Days.

nonimplacitando.c: NON Implacitando ali quern de liber tenemento fine breve, is a Writ to inhibit Bayliffs, &c. from distraining any Man without the Kings Writ, touching his Free - hold.

nonintromittendo.c: NON Intromittendo, quando breve de Pracipe in Capite fubdole impetratur, is a Writ directed to the Justices of the Bench, or in Eyre, willing them not to give one that hath, under colour of In - titling the King to Land, &c. as holding of him in Capite, deceitfully obtained the Writ called Pr recipe in Capite, but to put him to this Writ of Right, if he think good to use it.

nonmercandi.c: NON Mercandi and ViHualia, is a Writ di - reded to the Justices of Affile, commanding them to enquire, Whether the Officers of such Towns do well Viduals in Gross, or by Retail, during theif Office, contrary to the Statute, and to punish them if they find it true.

nonmoleftando.c: NON Moleftando, is a Writ that lieth for him which is Motefted, contrary to the King ’ s Prote - dion granted him.

nonobftante.c: NON Obftante, is a Clause frequent in Sta - tutes and Letters Patent it signifies Notvoithjland - ing, and was first brought in by the Pope, and in the Reign of Hen.. was used by that King in his Grants, & c.

nonponendk.c: NON Ponendk in AJftfis & Juratis, is a Writ founded upon the Statute of Weft,. cap.. and Articuli super Chartas, cap.. which is granted upon divers Causes to Men, for the freeing them from Affixes and Jurors.

nonprocedendo.c: NON Procedendo ad AJJifam Rege inconfultol is a Writ to flop the Trial of a Cause appertain - ing unto one that is in the King ’ s Service, until the King ’ s Plealure be further known.

nonreftdentiaproclericisregis.c: NON Reftdentia pro Clericis Regis, is a Writ directed to the Ordinary, charging him not to molest a Clerk employed in the King ’ s Service, by reason of his Non - Reft dence.

nonsanememory.c: NON Sane Memory, in Law, is an Exception taken to an Ad declared by the Plaintiff or De - mandant, to be done by another, whereupon he grounds his Plaint or Demands: And the Effed of it is, That the Party that did that Ad was Mad, or not well in his Wits when he did it. See Non compos mentis.

nonsolvendopecuniam.c: NON Solvendo Pecuniam ad quam Clericus tnulttatur pro non Reftdentia, is a Writ prohibit - ing an Ordinary to take a Pecuniary Muld im - posed upon a Clerk of the King, for Ncn - Rest - dence.

nonsuminformat.c: NON Sum Informat us. See Informatus non Sum.

nontenure.c: NON Tenure, in Law, is an Exception to a Count, by saying. That he holdeth not the Land specified in the Count, or at least some part of: And ’ tis either Non tenure General, or Non tenure Special: The Special Tenure, is an Exception, al - wedging that he was not Tenant the Day when the Writ was purchased. Non tenure General, is when one denies himself ever to have been Te - nant to the Land in Question, ' normal; N U M

normal.c: NORMAL, the fame with Perpendicular, or at Right Angles, and ’ tis usually spoken of a Line or a Plane that Interferes another Perpendicularly.. NORTHERN Signs of the Eclipticlgor odtac are those Six which constitute that Semi - circle, of the Ecliptick which inclines to the Northward from the Equator, as Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Can - cer, Leo, Virgo.,

nosocomium.c: NOSOCOMIUM, is an Hospital for Poor Sick People, where they are attended, and cured, if podible.

notesinmusick.c: NOTES in Musick, are certain Terms invent - ted to distinguish the Degrees of Sound in Tuning, and the Proportion of Time thereto belonging: For in regard that a Voice doth express a found best, when it pronounceth some Syllable or Word with it, fix select Syllables were formerly used to that purpose, ascending and descending in order, vi, Jt, fe, Mi, Fa, Sol, La j but four of them, vi. Mi, Fa, Sol, La, being found Suf - scient for the right Tuning of all the Degrees or Sound, and less burthenfome to the Memory, the other two, Vt and Re, are generally now laid aside as superfluous. It is reported, That Guido Aretinus, having undertaken to reduce the Greek. Scale of Musick to a more regular form a - bout A. D., assumed for the Names of these fix Notes as many Syllables taken out the Sap - thick. Hymn of St. John Ba. pt ist, which began thus: Ut queant Laxis RE fonare fibrisi MI ra Geflorum FKmiili tuorum, SOLve poUuti ' LKhii reatum. As for other fort of Notes relating to Time, they are Nine in Number, viz. Large, Long, Breve, Semi - breve, Minim, Crotchet, Quaver, Semi - quaver, and Detni - semi - quaver. The four first are usually termed Notes of Augmentation, or Increase, and the five last of Diminution or Decrease. The Se - mi - breve being the last of Augmentation, is com - monly called the Master - Note, or Measure - Note, or Time - Note, because it is of a, certain determin - name Measure or Length of Time by it self; and all the other Notes both of Augmentation and Diminution, are measured by, or adjusted to its value: But it ought to be observed, that the Large and Long are now of little use, as being too long for any Voice orlnftrument ( th c Organ only excepted ) to hold out to their full length; altho ’ their Bpfts are still very often used, more especially in Grave Musick, and Songs of many Parts.

noth.c: NOTH costa, are the five lowest Ribs on each side, called Bastard Ribs; so named because they do not join with the Breast - bone as the other Ribs do, nor are they as the others, Boney, but Cartilaginous. Diseases are likewise called Nothi, or Bastard, when they agree not with the Ordinary and Com - mon Rules, as Tertian, Quartan, and Quotidian, Bastard Agues, Bastard Pleuriftes, & C.

novacula.c: NOVACULA, is a Chirurgeon ’ s Knife, the Shape whereof differs according to the difference of Operations.

noveldijfeifin.c: NOVEL Dijfeifin. See Affile of Novel Dist ’ seisin.

nouns.c: NOUNS ( in Grammar ) are such Words as signifie the several Objects of our Thoughts.

nubecul.c: NUBECUL are little light Particles which mutually, but loosely close with one another, and swim upon the Urine.

nucamentuminphytology.c: NUCAMENTUM in Phytology, or Botanicfs, is the fame with Julus. Which fee.

nucha.c: NUCHA is the hinder part, or Nape of the Neck, called also Cervix.

nuciferousplantsorshrubs.c: NUCIFEROUS Plants or Shrubs are such a bear Nuts.

nuckianglandules.c: NUCKIAN Glandules, are a fore of Glands ( first taken notice of by Dr. Nucft ) seated in that Orbit of the Skull, wherein the Eye is placed betwixt the abducent Muscle of the Eye, and the upper part of the Os jugate. Their scrape is, various, in some Oblong, in others flatdfhly Round, in others Oval, and in others somewhat Triangular.

nucleus.c: NUCLEUS is the Edible part of the Kernel of any Nut, which is contained within the Skin of the Kernel; and in a larger sense is by Bora - mists used for any Fruit or Seed contained within an Husk or Shell.
NUCLEUS also in an Astronomical Sense is by Heveiius and others used for the Head of a Comet, and by others for the Central Parts of any Planets.

nucleusinarchitecture.c: NUCLEUS, in Architecture, is the middle part of the Flooring of the Ancients, consisting of Cement, which they put betwixt a Lay or Bed of Pebbles cemented with Mortar made of Lime and Sand.

nudecontrast.c: NUDE Contrast, in Law, is a bare Promile of a thing, without any consideration; and therefore ’ tis said, Ex nudo patio non oritur aSiio.

nudematter.c: NUDE Matter, in Common Law, is a naked Allegation of a thing done to be proved only by Witnesses, and not either by Record or other Specialty in Writing under Seal.

number.c: NUMBER is Discrete Quantity, or a Colle - stion of Unites, and is that which teacheth us to know how many any of the Objects of our Know - ledge are. Every Number in Arithmetic ! ( which is the Art of Numbering truly ) may be considered as composed of two Parts, or which one may be. called the Denominator, and the other the Name - razor. Thus the Number, as it signifies the Thing Numbered, as - the Mufes, or Men, Pounds, ( c. is a Denominator: But as it expresses how many of that thing are taken or accounted, it is a Numerator. Therefore when the Denominator signifies a whole thing, the Number is called an Integer; but if it signifie o i stand for the Parts of any thing, then the Number is a Fra St ion. Thus Nine Shillings, considered as diftindfc Things, are an Integral Number but when yon conder them as Parts of a Pound Sterling, that Number is a Fraction: And the Knowledge of this will facilitate the Understanding of the ' DcSlrine of Fractions, which appears difficult to Beginners, because they do not confider that as well Integer Numbers as Fractions have both Nu mercators and Denominators: The Difference ly - ing chiefly here, That in Integers the fatly of the Denominators is certain, one and the fame j but ' in N Y M in Fractions ' tis innumerable: For the Ratio of the Denominators in Fractions is as various as the Nature of the Parts into which any Whole may be divided, which in Vulgar Fractions is Infinite. Well ’ s Arithmetic.

numerationinarithmetick.c: NUMERATION in Arithmetick, is the true Distinction, Ejlimation, and Pronunciation of Num - bers, or the Rule to read any Number, tho ’ never so great, and to have a distinct Idea of each Place or Figure of it; which may easily be done ' by this Method: Beginning at the Right Hand, make a Point or Prick under the Seventh Figure, and over it place the Figure i, that is the Place of Millions. Now Seven Places any one can num - ber or read, but they are apt to be pulled when they go farther but ‘ tis as easie to read Places as Seven, if you do but go in this Me - tho; Accounting in the Seventh Place, over which you put the Figure, tell on Seven Places more, and over that place the Figure. The Number under, stands in the place of Millions of Millions, which is better expressed by Billions, ( i. e. Bi - millions. ) Including the last Figure, tell on again Seven Figures more, and then place o - ver the Seventh the Figure; this is the Place of Trillions and the Seventh beyond that will be Quarti / lions; the next Seventh Quin quill ions, cc. according as the Figures over every Seventh Place do sinew. Thus, suppose this Number, After yoii have distinguished it, as you fee, by the Pricks under, and ejiimated it by the Figures over it; you will find the ftift Period, beginning at the Left Hand, and reading to the Point, to be thousand; and you cannot be igno - rant of the Value of Nine, the last Figure, when you see the standing over it; for that hews you Stis Nonillions, or the Place of a Million mul - tiplied times by it self. The next Period is Thousand Octillions; the next is Thousand Septil lions; and so on till you have read or pronounced them aH: Only observing to express at every Point the Value of the Figure over it, which the Figure on the top shews you readily how to do.

numerator.c: NUMERATOR of a Fra & ion, is that Part of it which shews or numbers how many of those Parts which any Integer is supposed to be divided into, are expressed by the Fra & ion. Thus in f, is the Numerator, ( which stands always above the Line; and ( hews you, that if any Whole be divided into Parts, you number and enumerate, or take of them, /. e. Three quarters.

numeralalgebra.c: NUMERAL Algebra, is that which makes use of Numbers instead of the Letters of the Alpha - bet; which latter Method is called Algebra in Spc cies, or Specious Arithmetic,

nuperobi.c: NUPER Obi it, is a Writ that lies for a Co - heir, being deforced by her Co - parcener of Lands or Tenements, whereof any of their Ancestors died seized of an Estate in Fee - simple. N USANCE, a Term in Law, signifying not only a Thing done, whereby another Man is an - noted in his Free Lands or Tenements, but the Assise or Writ which lieth for the fame; and now generally, instead of this, is brought in A - dions of Trespass.

nutrition.c: NUTRITION, is a Natural Increase, where - by that which continually decays of any Corpo - real Substance, is repaired by convenient Nou - rifhment. Dr. Havers, in his OJleologia, will not have Nutrition to be any Reparation of the Loss of the Substance of the Solid Parts ordinarily, but only a continual Succession and Supply of Spirits, and of all those Fluid Parts which fill the con - gaining Parts, and keep them distended.

NUTRITION. The Course or Process of the Aliment in order to the Nourishment and Support of an Humane Body, is thus performed, ihe Meat we eat being grosly divided and ground by the Teeth, [ s in that action mingled withJthe Sa - live, which helps to ferment and dilute it. hence thro ’ the Osfophagus or Gullet by the conftridion of its Fibres ’ tis thrust down into the Stomach where being further softened and swell ’ d by the Juices contained in the Glands of the Stomach, its n y m j Parrs are farther broken and the intimate Cohesion of them destroyed, and they divided one from a - nother, by the peipetuai motion of the Coats of the Stomach and by the Muscles of the Midrif j and Abdomen. By this preffttre also of the Sides or the Stomach upon the contained Aliment, that is thrust down into the Intestines at its entry in - to which it is mix ’ d with the Bile and Pancreatick Juice, the one to sweeten, the other to dilute the Chyle. By the Perifialticl Vermicular motion of the Guts, ( arising from the Alternate A & ion of their Spiral and Longitudinal Fibres ) and by the pressure of the Diaphragm, and the Muscles of the Abdomen, the grosser parts of the Chyle are deri - ved downwards to be thrust out of the Body; whi ’ e the finer are squeezed into tape narrow Oral fices of the Lacteal Veins, which opens into the In - testiness; from whence in slender Channels they are carried into the Glands of the Mesentery; where they receive a fine thin Lympha from the Lymphatic f Dulls, which further dilates it and scour its containing Vessels; which Vessels going from those Mefenterick Glands unite into larger Channels, and those into still larger, and at last pass directly into the common Receptacle of the Chyle; which is a kind of Bason formed for it in the. union of thele Lacleal and Lymphatick Ves - self. From thence in one Dud it ascends into the Thorax, and sometimes dividing about the Heart, it immediately unites again, and creeping along the Gullet, it passes on to the jest Subclavian Vein, where in one or two Months it pours in its Contents, and there mixes with the poor Venal Blood returning from all parts of the Body. And thus doth the Blood receive its Supply and Nou -, riihment. But if you take Nutrition in the Sense which feme do, of rhe Blood nounfiling the several parts of the Body: Then will that kind of Nutrition be performed by a Secretory Dull arising from the Termination of an Artery, and carrying a suitable portion of the Blood to every part to be nourifii - ed; so that every Point of the Body must be the ' Termination of a Secretory Duel thro ’ which a pro - per part of the Blood is brought in order to sup - ply that part of the Body.

nux.c: NUX is a fort of Pain in the Head, which assai & s a Place as big as a Nut; as an Ovum or Clavus is another fort, where the Seat of the Pain is larger.

nychthemeron.c: NYCHTHEMERON, is Four and twenty Hours Space, or an entire Day and Night.

nyctalopia.c: NYCTALOPIA is Two - fold: The First is a Dimness of the Sight in the Night, or in dark Places, without any Impediment in the Light. The other is Dimness in the Light, and clear Sight in the Night, or in Shady Places.

nympha.c: NYMPHA, are little soft Pieces of Flesh, ari - sing from the Commissure of the Os pubis with - in the Vagina; so called, because they stand near the Passage of the Water that comes out of the Bladder. Also the Hollowness or void Space in the Ne - ther Lip is so called.

noveltyofservices.c: NOVELTY of Services, in Law, signifies Equa - lity of Services as when the Tenant Paravail owes as much to the Mesne, as the Mesne does to the Lord Paramount.

nitreinarchitecture.c: NITRE, in Architecture, is the Workmens Term for an Angle that is just degrees, or half a right one; and if it be a quarter of ’ a Right Angle they call it a Half Nitre: And they have an Instrument made to this Angle which they call the Nitre Square, with which they strike Nitre Lines on their Quarters or Battens; and for dispatch they have a Nitre Box, as they call it, which is made of two pieces of Wood, each about an Inch thick, and one is nailed upright upon the Edge of the other; the upper piece hath theMitre Lines struck upon it on both sides, and a Kerf to direct the Saw in Cutting the Nitre Joints readily, by only applying the piece into this Box.

native.c: NATIVE habendo, was a Writ that lay to the Sheriff, for a Lord, whose Villain claimed for his Inheritance, run from him, for the apprehending and restoring him to his Lord again.

noisenativa.c: NOISE, Nativa is a Bond - woman. An. E.. and R.. cap. z. But if file married a Free - man she was thereby made free; and when once made free and discharged of all Bondage cannot be Neife after, without some special Ad done by her; as Divorce or Confession in a Court of Re - cord. Nor shall a Free - woman be bound by taking a Villain to her Husband; but their Issue shall be Villains after their Father. There was also anciently a Writ of Neifty whereby the Lord claim ’ d his Neife - but all this is now out of doors.

nomination.c: NOMINATION this word as well by the Canonifts as Common Lawyers, is used for a Power that a Man hath by vertue of a Manner or otherwise, of appointing or naming a Clerk to a Patron of a Benefice, to be by him presented to the Ordinary.

norroyornorth.c: NORROY, or North - poy, i. e. the Northern King is the Title of the Third of the three Kings at Arms in the Heralds Office. His Province lies on the North - side of T rent.

novation.c: NOVATION, in the Civil Law, is a transfer - ring the first Obligation given by a Debtor to a Creditor, into another.
